transcript.content: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. I've been having this issue where during long meetings at work, people will talk directly to me and I just completely zone out. I only realize afterward that I didn't actually hear or process what they were saying, and it's starting to really affect my job.
Have you experienced these episodes of 'zoning out' since you were a child, or is this a relatively new development that started later in your life?

The severe zoning out is relatively new and really came to a head over the last two years since my company restructured and my meeting load increased. When I was a child, my struggles were actually the opposite; my elementary school teachers always complained that I was constantly out of my seat, talking over classmates, and couldn't sit still. So the physical restlessness was there early on, but this mental drifting in meetings is much more recent.

During these episodes of 'zoning out,' do you feel as though you are detached from your body or that your surroundings seem unreal, or does it feel more like your mind is simply wandering and unable to stay focused on the speaker?

It is definitely just my mind wandering rather than any feeling of detachment or things not being real. I will be looking directly at the person speaking, but my brain has drifted off to mundane thoughts like what I'm going to make for dinner. Then I suddenly snap out of it and realize I have no idea what they just said or how to respond.

Beyond the zoning out in meetings, do you still find yourself frequently interrupting others, struggling to wait your turn, or feeling a persistent, restless need to be physically active or moving in your daily life?

Yes, I constantly feel this wired, crawling restlessness inside when forced to sit still, which leads to me pacing the office and staying busy at home instead of ever relaxing. I also frequently blurt out answers in meetings or finish people's sentences, and I feel so embarrassed afterward when I realize I've interrupted them. It's like I just can't stop myself from moving or talking.

Looking back at your childhood and adolescence, were there any significant periods where your hyperactivity or impulsivity noticeably decreased, or has that restless, 'wired' feeling been a constant presence throughout your life?

That restless, 'wired' feeling has been a constant presence since my childhood without any breaks. Even in elementary school, teachers always complained about me being out of my seat and talking over classmates. I used to manage it better by keeping active and organizing things around my own rhythms, but it's become much more of a struggle lately.

Since your childhood, have you consistently experienced both significant inattentive symptoms and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms, or were there periods where your focus was generally good despite the restlessness?

When I was younger, my focus and grades were actually quite good, and my issues were almost entirely hyperactive and impulsive. Throughout most of my adult life, I kept my focus manageable by organizing my work around my own rhythms. It was only over the last two years, with the company restructuring and those endless meetings, that the severe zoning out became a major problem alongside my lifelong restlessness.

Looking back at your life, would you say that you have consistently met the criteria for both significant inattention and significant hyperactivity-impulsivity simultaneously, or has the inattention primarily emerged as a major struggle only recently?

The hyperactivity and impulsivity have definitely been constant since childhood, back when I'd get in trouble in school for not sitting still or waiting my turn. The severe inattention and zoning out, however, have only become a major struggle in the last two years. Before my new role forced me into these long, passive meetings, I was always able to work at my own dynamic pace, so my focus never seemed like an issue.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a lifelong history of persistent hyperactivity and impulsivity (meeting criteria since childhood) and current symptoms of inattention that have become clinically significant in the context of recent environmental demands. As the hyperactive-impulsive symptoms have been the predominant and constant feature throughout the patient's life, the combined presentation or predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation is supported.
